title: What they ask about
hookLine: they ask about wine and gambling, and about orphans, and each gets a plain answer (2:219–220)

cards: Scroll through any community's question board and you learn who they are. A parents' group: is this rash normal? A new neighborhood: where do I put the recycling?
The questions are small and real and a little anxious. Al-Baqarah has a question board too. Again and again, a verse begins: they ask you.
What people asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ shows who they were: a young community trying to live well. Today: what they ask about.

teach.b: Yas'alunaka: they ask you. In al-Baqarah alone, the phrase comes again and again: about the new moons, about what to spend and on whom, about fighting in the sacred month.
In verses two hundred nineteen and two hundred twenty, three questions in a row.
They ask about wine and gambling. The answer: in both is great sin and some benefit for people, but, in Pickthall's words, “the sin of them is greater than their usefulness.”
It doesn't pretend there's no benefit; it weighs.

They ask what they should spend. The answer is one word, al-'afw: the surplus, what you can spare beyond your needs. Then they ask about orphans, and here the commentators tell the story behind the question.
Abu Dawud records, from Ibn Abbas, that verses warning sternly against consuming orphans' wealth had come down, and guardians got scared.
They began cooking an orphan's food separately, and if any was left over, they kept it apart until it spoiled. Everyone was miserable, and the orphan ate stale food. So they asked.

teach.h: ORPHANS: WHAT IS GOOD FOR THEM
teach.b: The answer is plain: doing what is good for them is best; if you share your life with them, they are your brothers; God knows the one who spoils from the one who sets right.
In the report, fear had made the rule harder than it was, a little like the cow. The answer cuts to the point: not whether the rule was followed perfectly, but whether the orphan is better off.

how: Islamic law forbids alcohol and gambling, encourages charity from what one can spare, and treats care of orphans as a weighty duty; guardians may share household life with orphans as long as they act for the orphan's good.

o: they ask you: the opening of many of al-Baqarah's answers
a command to answer every question you're asked
a list of things forbidden to the early Muslims

games.q: questions and answers — tap the pairs.
p: the sin is greater than the use
the surplus, what you can spare
what is good for them is best

s: the answer about wine and gambling says they have no benefit at all
it says there is some benefit, but the sin is greater.
guardians once cooked orphans' food separately out of fear, until it spoiled
Abu Dawud records it from Ibn Abbas; 2:220 answered them.

games.q: you're a guardian, terrified of touching an orphan's wealth, so you cook their food apart and it spoils. you ask the Prophet. what's the answer?
o: do what is good for them; if you share your life, they're your brothers.
give the orphan to someone else.
games.why: what is good for them is best. fear had made the rule harder than it was; the answer cut through to the orphan's good.

practice: Think of a question someone keeps asking you, out loud or with their eyes, a child, a partner, a colleague, that you've answered with something long and defensive, or not at all.
Ask what is actually good for them, and find the plain answer in one or two sentences.

wordCard.voice: Yas'alunaka. They ask you — the phrase that opens al-Baqarah's answers on wine, gambling, spending and orphans. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: good for them is best. Fear can make a rule harder than it is. Until tomorrow.
